concepts.name: Big-O notation
concepts.gloss: Asymptotic upper bounds on growth of functions up to constant factors.

concepts.name: Polynomials
concepts.gloss: Expressions Σ aₖ xᵏ with coefficient lists, added and multiplied in the usual way.

concepts.name: Complex numbers
concepts.gloss: Numbers a+bi with i²=−1, including roots of unity e^{2πij/k}.

concepts.name: Multitape Turing machine
concepts.gloss: A Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed number of one-dimensional tapes, each head moving at most one cell per step.

evidence.quote: A machine has one fixed finite alphabet and one fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes.

concepts.name: n log n optimality conjecture
concepts.gloss: Schönhage and Strassen's 1971 conjecture that n log n is the optimal order of growth for multiplying n-bit integers on a multitape Turing machine.

evidence.quote: Sch\"onhage and Strassen conjectured $n\log n$ as the optimal order of multiplication cost
and proposed $n\log n$ as the optimal order of growth

concepts.name: Harvey–van der Hoeven O(n log n) multiplier
concepts.gloss: The established fixed-tape integer multiplier running in O(n log n) time, used here only as an ordinary subroutine for short polynomial products.

evidence.quote: Harvey and van der Hoeven reached the unconditional $O(n\log n)$ upper bound
Calls to the established $O(n\log n)$ multiplier are ordinary subroutine calls; they do not invoke the improved theorem recursively.

concepts.name: Normalized discrete Fourier transform
concepts.gloss: The map F_q sending a length-q complex vector u to (1/q)Σ u_j e^{−2πijk/q}, a contraction with a signed inverse F_q⁺.

evidence.quote: Each normalized Fourier transform above is a contraction, since each output averages inputs multiplied by complex numbers of modulus one.

concepts.name: Cyclic convolution
concepts.gloss: The product of coefficient arrays indexed by a cyclic group (polynomial product modulo x^S − 1), which the Fourier transform turns into pointwise multiplication.

evidence.quote: Thus convolution modulo $x^S-1$ has no nonzero wraparound.

concepts.name: Multidimensional Fourier transform
concepts.gloss: The tensor product of one-dimensional normalized Fourier transforms applied along each axis of an array on a product of cyclic groups.

evidence.quote: it replaces the Fourier transforms needed for this convolution by multidimensional transforms whose axis lengths are powers of two.

concepts.name: Radix-digit reduction to convolution
concepts.gloss: Splitting each n-bit input into radix-2^b digits turns integer multiplication into convolution of short integer coefficient lists followed by carry propagation.

evidence.quote: Splitting the inputs into radix digits reduces multiplication to convolution of short integer coefficients.
Write the two inputs as polynomials in $2^b$, each with $q=\lceil n/b\rceil$ nonnegative digits.

concepts.name: Arrays on tape and logical volume
concepts.gloss: Arrays with address set [a₁]×…×[a_t] are stored in lexicographic order with implicit addresses; V, the logical volume, is the number of stored data bits, and rows are contiguous blocks at a fixed prefix and row index.

evidence.quote: The \emph{logical volume} $V$ is the number of stored data bits.
An address is implicit in an entry's position in this ordered stream; it is not stored beside every data bit.

concepts.name: Elementary stream operations
concepts.gloss: Linear-time O(V) tape operations: permuting or moving a single radix digit, splitting and merging streams by a digit, and distributing rows cyclically among a fixed number of streams.

evidence.quote: Each of the following operations on an array of volume $V$ takes $O(V)$ steps on a fixed number of one-dimensional tapes

concepts.name: Controlled shifts and rational scalings
concepts.gloss: Updating a target address field y ↦ y + a(controls) mod q^b, or multiplying it by a fixed rational unit, in O(V) time when the target field follows its control fields.

evidence.quote: The next operations are linear because their target field follows their control fields.

concepts.name: Linear network with wire roles
concepts.gloss: A fixed finite circuit of wires carrying scalars and gates applying fixed linear maps; a wire's fixed place is its role, and auxiliary scratch wires may start with arbitrary values.

evidence.quote: A wire's fixed place in the network is called its role.
A gate is a fixed linear map on a specified set of wires; untouched wires retain their values.

concepts.name: Restoration of arbitrary scratch values
concepts.gloss: An eight-row schedule that subtracts the effect of old scratch values, adds the source's effect, then undoes the copies, so the net change y ← y + x is independent of the scratch contents, which are restored.

evidence.quote: This cancellation of arbitrary initial scratch values is a linear instance of the restoration construction for transparent computation

concepts.name: Triple-intersection bank exchange
concepts.gloss: Two networks indexed by three-element subsets of [100], where gather/scatter through central wires produce coefficients depending on intersection size and side wires cancel the unwanted ones, giving y ← y + x; three stages then exchange banks (X,Y) ↦ (−Y,X).

evidence.quote: The construction uses three-element subsets: gather and scatter create coefficients depending on intersection size, and auxiliary wires cancel the unwanted coefficients.
and restores every auxiliary value.  In the bit construction this is the permutation exchanging $X_a$ and $Y_a$.

concepts.name: Frames and the common-frame identity
concepts.gloss: Each source, gate and sink carries an invertible linear operator D_v on wire arrays; because a common frame commutes with a pointwise gate, the network applied to arrays implements D_out·S·D_in⁻¹, so only endpoint frames matter.

evidence.quote: We call $D_v$ its frame: the stored array is $D_vg$ when the logical array is $g$.
Thus the common frame commutes with the pointwise gate, and the invariant continues to the sinks.

concepts.name: Nested subspace labels and orthogonal residuals
concepts.gloss: Each gate and terminal is labelled by a nondegenerate subspace of a fixed m-dimensional bilinear space, nested along edges; the orthogonal residual of an edge measures how many smaller operations its frame change needs.

evidence.quote: A label is a nondegenerate subspace of a fixed bilinear space.
the orthogonal complement of the smaller label inside the larger one; its dimension is the absolute change in label dimension.

concepts.name: Rank deficit s < Wm
concepts.title: Rank deficit $s < Wm$

symbols.name: smaller-call count
symbols.meaning: The total number of smaller recursive calls needed on all network edges (sum of edge ranks or residual dimensions).

symbols.name: wire count
symbols.meaning: The number of wires (roles) in the fixed network, including scratch wires.

symbols.name: label dimension
symbols.meaning: The dimension of the ambient label space, the number of address fields per chunk handled by one recursion level (here 10⁶).

concepts.gloss: The decisive property of both networks: the total number s of smaller calls needed on all edges is strictly less than the wire count W times the label dimension m.

evidence.quote: The decisive property is that the total number $s$ of smaller calls satisfies $s<Wm$.

concepts.name: Recursive power saving
concepts.gloss: A call at parameter mf is done by s calls at parameter f on streams of volume V/W, so normalized cost grows by s/W < m^τ per level, giving cost O(V·f^τ) with τ < 1.

evidence.quote: A recursive call at parameter $mf$ therefore uses $s$ calls at parameter $f$, each on a stream of volume $V/W$.
This strict inequality is the source of the power saving.

concepts.name: Lower triangular factorization
concepts.gloss: Every rational m×m matrix of rank a factors as E₁ Π E₂ with E₁,E₂ invertible lower triangular and Π a partial permutation with a ones (a reversed-order Bruhat factorization).

evidence.quote: Every rational $m\times m$ matrix $A$ of rank $a$ has a factorization

concepts.name: Address shear
concepts.gloss: The address permutation (H,D) ↦ (H+MD, D) on two groups of m digit fields over ℤ/q^bℤ; a matrix of rank a is performed with exactly a smaller field interchanges plus O(V) work.

evidence.quote: For the bit procedure, that endpoint operator is an address shear:
can be performed with exactly $a$ interchanges of pairs of $b$-digit fields and $O(V)$ further work.

concepts.name: Bit network interface
concepts.gloss: The XOR network with projection frames Φ_{P_U}: each route's endpoint matrices differ by the identity, so every role receives the shear H ← H + D, while the edge ranks sum to s_b < W_b·m.

evidence.quote: The bit network has $W_{\rm b}$ wires, uses only pointwise XOR gates, and sends its input vector to the permutation $\rho$ of that vector.

concepts.name: Fast address-chunk interchange
concepts.gloss: Interchanging two disjoint contiguous address fields of u bits in an array costs O(V·u^τ) with τ = 1 − 2⁻⁵⁰, realized by recursively applying the bit network and computing XOR combinations of data.

evidence.quote: The first procedure interchanges two disjoint contiguous address fields of $u$ bits in an array whose addresses form a complete Cartesian product.
Its cost is $O(Vu^\tau)$ for a fixed $\tau<1$.

concepts.name: Normalized butterfly H₀
concepts.title: Normalized butterfly $H_0$

symbols.name: normalized butterfly
symbols.meaning: The 2×2 map sending a pair (u,v) to ((u+v)/2,(u−v)/2).

concepts.gloss: The two-point map H₀(u,v) = ((u+v)/2, (u−v)/2), the basic step of radix-two Fourier transforms, applied coefficientwise to polynomial records.

evidence.quote: simultaneously on selected coordinate bits of the numerical arrays.

concepts.name: Gaussian dyadic numbers
concepts.gloss: Complex numbers in ℤ[i,1/2], whose real and imaginary parts have power-of-two denominators; intermediate values of the numerical procedure are kept exactly in this form.

evidence.quote: Intermediate values are exact Gaussian dyadics, whose real and imaginary parts have power-of-two denominators.

concepts.name: Polynomial ring modulo y^r + 1
concepts.title: Polynomial ring modulo $y^r + 1$

symbols.name: polynomial variable
symbols.meaning: The indeterminate of the polynomial records, whose powers act as roots of unity.

symbols.name: record length
symbols.meaning: The number of complex coefficients in each polynomial record, a power of two.

concepts.gloss: The ring ℂ[y]/(y^r+1) with r a power of two, where multiplication by a power of y is a signed shift of the coefficient list, so powers of y serve as cheap roots of unity.

evidence.quote: is stored as the coefficient list of a polynomial modulo $y^r+1$, with $r$ a power of two.
multiplication by such a root is a signed shift of the coefficient list.

concepts.name: Fixed-point disk grid and truncation
concepts.gloss: Values are stored as complex numbers in the unit disk with real and imaginary parts on the grid 2^{−p}ℤ, and Q_p truncation toward that grid adds error below √2·2^{−p}.

evidence.quote: A $p$-bit grid array has real and imaginary coefficient parts in $2^{-p}\mathbb Z$.

concepts.name: Binary phase frames
concepts.gloss: For the complex network, frames C_U = H^{⊗m} diag(i^{wt(P_U x) mod 4}) H^{⊗m}; an edge's frame change is a product of one two-point kernel aI + bX_v per orthonormal residual vector, and telescoping gives the kernel C^{⊗m} on every role.

evidence.quote: is a product of one translation kernel $aI+bX_v$, or its inverse, per vector in an orthonormal basis of the edge residual.

concepts.name: Simultaneous butterfly layer
concepts.gloss: Applying H₀ on the same bit position in each of up to d equal-width address chunks costs O(V·d^λ′) with λ′ < 1, by recursing through the complex network's phase frames, with exact dyadic intermediates and one final truncation.

evidence.quote: one selects the same bit position in each of at most $d$ equal-width address chunks, and the cost is $O(Vd^{\lambda'})$ for a fixed $\lambda'<1$.
A single truncation follows the completed contractive layer.

concepts.name: Synthetic polynomial transform
concepts.gloss: Nussbaumer's Fourier transform over ℂ[y]/(y^r+1) using ω_t = y^{2r/t} as root of unity, computed by decimation-in-frequency butterflies and signed shifts, with outputs left in bit-reversed frequency order.

evidence.quote: These are the synthetic polynomial transforms of Nussbaumer and Quandalle and Nussbaumer
In this representation, the transform calculation consists of address rearrangements, signed shifts, and two-point butterfly operations.

concepts.name: Fast synthetic transform layout
concepts.gloss: A tape layout placing the selected bits of participating axes at a common offset in consecutive K-bit chunks so simultaneous butterfly layers apply, with chunk interchanges paying for the movement.

evidence.quote: we must place the selected bits of the participating axes at a common offset in consecutive $K$-bit chunks.

concepts.name: Signed Kronecker packing
concepts.gloss: Multiplying two polynomial records by packing their signed integer coefficients into one large integer, multiplying with the O(n log n) multiplier, and unpacking, in O(rp log(rp)) time.

evidence.quote: Signed coefficient packing is a form of Kronecker substitution

concepts.name: Normalized convolution over the polynomial ring
concepts.gloss: Cyclic convolution of arrays with values in ℂ[y]/(y^r+1), computed by two forward synthetic transforms kept in stored frequency order, packed pointwise ring products, and the opposite transform.

evidence.quote: The two forward synthetic transforms retain the same frequency order through their pointwise product, and the opposite transform consumes that order.

concepts.name: Coefficient twist
concepts.gloss: The phase twist x ↦ ζy with ζ = e^{πi/r}, mapping ℂ[x]/(x^r−1) isomorphically onto ℂ[y]/(y^r+1), so cyclic convolution in the last coordinate becomes negacyclic polynomial arithmetic.

evidence.quote: A phase twist changes the last cyclic coordinate into a polynomial modulo $y^r+1$; its negative wrap gives precisely the original cyclic wrap after the twist is removed.

concepts.name: Gaussian resampling with retained permutations
concepts.gloss: Harvey–van der Hoeven's identity expressing a Fourier transform of prime length s through one of power-of-two length t (P_sF_s = 2^{2α²} B₀ P_t F_t A), here with both coordinate permutations kept in the formula instead of sorted.

evidence.quote: Gaussian resampling then expresses each source Fourier transform through a power-of-two tensor transform.
We retain both permutations in the transform formula and compute that formula directly.

concepts.name: Bluestein chirp identity
concepts.gloss: Rewriting a Fourier transform (with its target permutation) as pointwise multiplication by a chirp, a cyclic convolution with the chirp, and another chirp multiplication.

evidence.quote: Next, Bluestein's chirp identity converts the middle transform, including its target permutation, into normalized cyclic convolution.

concepts.name: Chinese-remainder address map
concepts.gloss: A convolution-preserving map placing the radix-digit coefficient list on a product of distinct prime-length cyclic axes, implemented by triangular controlled shifts and axis moves.

evidence.quote: First, the radix-digit coefficient list is placed on a product of distinct prime cyclic axes by a Chinese-remainder map that preserves convolution.

concepts.name: Exact coefficient recovery and carries
concepts.gloss: Removing known normalizations and digit scales, showing the computed coefficient error is below 1/2 so rounding gives exact integers, then propagating carries to obtain the binary product.

evidence.quote: proves that the recovered coefficient error is strictly below $1/2$, and propagates carries to obtain the exact binary product.

concepts.name: Fixed rational parameters and cost table
concepts.gloss: The compatible choice τ = σ = 1 − 2⁻⁵⁰, λ′ = 1 − 2⁻⁵⁴, ε = 2⁻⁷⁵, κ = 2⁻¹⁸², etc., under which every term of the normalized cost table is O((lg n)^{1−κ}).

evidence.quote: A compatible choice of rational parameters makes all terms in its cost table fit Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
These constants are deliberately conservative; no optimization is claimed.

concepts.name: Integer multiplication below n log n
concepts.title: Integer multiplication in $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$ time

symbols.name: input bit length
symbols.meaning: The number of bits in each of the two input integers.

symbols.name: binary logarithm
symbols.meaning: The function lg n = max{⌈log₂ n⌉, 1}.

symbols.name: saving exponent
symbols.meaning: The fixed constant 2⁻¹⁸² by which the exponent of the logarithmic factor drops below one.

symbols.name: big-O
symbols.meaning: Asymptotic upper bound up to a constant factor.

concepts.gloss: A single deterministic fixed-alphabet multitape Turing machine multiplies two n-bit integers exactly in O(n (lg n)^{1−κ}) time with κ = 2⁻¹⁸², disproving the n log n optimality conjecture in this model.

evidence.quote: We give a deterministic algorithm that multiplies two $n$-bit integers in $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$ worst-case time
The algorithm is exact for every input length and disproves the $n\log n$ optimality conjecture of Sch\"onhage and Strassen in this model.

concepts.name: Asymptotic notation beyond big-O
concepts.gloss: Ω, Θ and o give asymptotic lower bounds, tight bounds and strictly smaller growth of functions, alongside big-O upper bounds.

concepts.name: Logarithms and exponents
concepts.gloss: The logarithm log_b x is the exponent to which b must be raised to get x; lg n here denotes the base-two logarithm rounded up.

concepts.name: Floor and ceiling
concepts.gloss: ⌊x⌋ is the largest integer at most x and ⌈x⌉ the smallest integer at least x.

concepts.name: Binary representation of integers
concepts.gloss: Writing a nonnegative integer as a sum of digits times powers of a radix such as 2, with the leftmost digit most significant.

concepts.name: Schoolbook integer arithmetic with carries
concepts.gloss: Adding and multiplying integers digit by digit, passing carries to higher positions, which multiplies n-bit numbers in O(n²) bit operations.

concepts.name: Two's complement and signed integers
concepts.gloss: Standard ways of representing negative integers in binary, so that addition, subtraction and sign changes are simple bit operations.

concepts.name: XOR and arithmetic modulo 2
concepts.gloss: The bit operation that is 1 exactly when its two inputs differ, which is addition of bits modulo 2.

concepts.name: Modular arithmetic
concepts.gloss: Arithmetic on integers where numbers are identified when their difference is divisible by a fixed modulus, so sums and products wrap around.

concepts.name: Prime numbers and gcd
concepts.gloss: A prime has no divisors other than 1 and itself; the gcd is the largest integer dividing two given integers, which are coprime when it is 1.

concepts.name: Euclidean algorithm
concepts.gloss: Repeated division with remainder that computes gcd(a,b) and, in its extended form, integers x,y with ax+by=gcd(a,b), giving inverses modulo b.

concepts.name: Chinese remainder theorem
concepts.gloss: For pairwise coprime moduli, a system of congruences has a unique solution modulo their product, so Z/(n₁n₂)Z corresponds to pairs of residues.

concepts.name: Binomial coefficients and subsets
concepts.gloss: C(n,k) counts the k-element subsets of an n-element set; subsets are combined with intersection, union and Cartesian product.

concepts.name: Permutations
concepts.gloss: A bijection from a finite set to itself, describing a reordering of items; permutations compose and have inverses.

concepts.name: Lexicographic order
concepts.gloss: Ordering tuples by their first coordinate, then by the second among ties, and so on, as for row-major storage of arrays.

concepts.name: Vectors and matrices
concepts.gloss: Rectangular arrays of numbers representing linear maps, multiplied by the row-times-column rule, with special forms such as identity, diagonal, permutation and triangular matrices.

concepts.name: Linear maps and invertibility
concepts.gloss: A map preserving sums and scalar multiples, given by a matrix; it is invertible when another linear map undoes it.

concepts.name: Vector spaces, subspaces and dimension
concepts.gloss: A set of vectors closed under linear combinations, with a dimension equal to the size of any basis; a subspace is such a set inside a larger one.

concepts.name: Rank of a matrix
concepts.gloss: The dimension of the space spanned by a matrix's columns, equal to that of its rows.

concepts.name: Dot product and orthogonality
concepts.gloss: The sum of coordinatewise products of two vectors; vectors are orthogonal when it is zero.

concepts.name: Gaussian elimination
concepts.gloss: Reducing a matrix by row operations to triangular or echelon form, used to solve linear systems and compute rank.

concepts.name: Fields and rings
concepts.gloss: Number systems with addition and multiplication obeying the usual laws; a field also has division by nonzero elements, as in Q, C or the integers modulo a prime.

concepts.name: Fast Fourier transform
concepts.gloss: The divide-and-conquer algorithm computing a length-n discrete Fourier transform in O(n log n) arithmetic operations by recursively combining half-length transforms with two-point butterflies.

concepts.name: Polynomial multiplication via evaluation and interpolation
concepts.gloss: Multiplying polynomials by evaluating them at roots of unity, multiplying values pointwise, and interpolating back, which the FFT makes O(n log n).

concepts.name: Bit-reversal permutation
concepts.gloss: The reordering of indices 0..2^k−1 that reverses the k-bit binary representation of each index, arising in in-place radix-two FFTs.

concepts.name: Karatsuba multiplication
concepts.gloss: Multiplying two n-digit numbers with three half-size products instead of four, giving O(n^{log₂3}) time.

concepts.name: Divide-and-conquer recurrences
concepts.gloss: Equations expressing an algorithm's cost on a problem through its cost on smaller subproblems, solved by unrolling or the master theorem.

concepts.name: Mathematical induction
concepts.gloss: Proving a statement for all natural numbers by proving a base case and that each case implies the next.

concepts.name: Geometric series
concepts.gloss: The sum a + ar + ar² + … , equal to a(1−r^k)/(1−r), bounded by a constant times its largest term when r is fixed away from 1.

concepts.name: Limits
concepts.gloss: The value a sequence approaches as its index grows; the limit inferior is the smallest value it keeps returning near.

concepts.name: Exponential function and Gaussians
concepts.gloss: The function e^x and its complex extension e^{iθ}=cosθ+i sinθ, including bell-shaped Gaussian functions e^{−cx²}.

concepts.name: Absolute value and the triangle inequality
concepts.gloss: The size |z| of a real or complex number, which satisfies |a+b| ≤ |a|+|b| and is used to bound accumulated errors.

concepts.name: Rounding to the nearest integer
concepts.gloss: Replacing a real number by the closest integer, which recovers an integer exactly when the approximation error is below 1/2.

concepts.name: Newton's method
concepts.gloss: An iteration x ↦ x − f(x)/f′(x) that roughly doubles the number of correct digits per step near a simple root, used for reciprocals and square roots.

concepts.name: Integer division and square root
concepts.gloss: For a,b>0, the unique q,r with a=bq+r and 0≤r<b, and the largest integer whose square is at most a.

concepts.name: Deterministic algorithm and worst-case running time
concepts.gloss: An algorithm whose steps are fixed by its input, measured by the maximum number of steps it takes over all inputs of a given length.

concepts.name: Stacks
concepts.gloss: A last-in first-out store; popping returns items in the reverse of the order they were pushed.

concepts.name: Binary counter
concepts.gloss: A register holding a number in binary that is incremented by flipping trailing ones and a zero, costing O(1) amortized bit flips per increment.

concepts.name: Hamming weight
concepts.gloss: The number of nonzero entries in a binary vector.

concepts.name: Matrix transposition
concepts.gloss: Rearranging an array so the entry at row i, column j moves to row j, column i.

concepts.name: Turing machine alphabet and simulation constants
concepts.gloss: A Turing machine's states and finite alphabet can encode several tracks or extra marks, and fixed changes of this kind change running time only by a constant factor.

background.summary: The reader has an undergraduate computer science education: discrete mathematics (sets, permutations, modular arithmetic, gcd and the Chinese remainder theorem, induction, binomial coefficients), the algorithms course (asymptotic notation, recurrences, Karatsuba, the FFT and FFT-based polynomial multiplication, bit-reversal, binary counters, stacks), introductory computability (Turing machines with multiple tapes and constant-factor simulations), and the supporting mathematics of a CS degree: calculus with limits, exponentials and Newton's method, complex numbers, and a first linear algebra course (matrices, rank, invertibility, subspaces, dimension, dot products and orthogonality over the reals, Gaussian elimination). They have not studied bilinear forms over general fields, tensor products of operators, Bruhat factorizations, algebraic complexity of integer multiplication beyond Karatsuba and the basic FFT, or research-level fast multiplication (Schönhage–Strassen, Fürer, Harvey–van der Hoeven, Nussbaumer transforms, Gaussian resampling), nor index coding or the Frankl–Wilson construction.
